Zwishenzug in chess means an in-between move — something unexpected or indirect played before the more obvious move — that disrupts an opponent’s plans. Applied to life, it’s doing a surprising, small or indirect action before the predictable/obvious next step in order to change others’ expectations or reduce resistance. Below are ten examples (mix of real events with sources and plausible made-up scenarios). For each I note why it’s a Zwishenzug-style move.

Real examples (with sources)

1) Operation Fortitude (Allied WWII deception before D‑Day)
- What happened: The Allies ran a large-scale deception (fake armies, double agents, false radio traffic) to convince Germany the invasion would be at Pas de Calais rather than Normandy.
- Why Zwishenzug: The deception was a surprise intermediate action played before the obvious invasion; it caused the enemy to commit forces away from the true objective.
- Source: UK National Archives / Imperial War Museum summary of Operation Fortitude — https://www.iwm.org.uk/history/operation-fortitude and https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/worldwar2/theatre-of-war/deceptions/

2) Google’s acquisition of Android (2005) before the smartphone race
- What happened: Google quietly acquired Android Inc. in 2005 and developed Android as an OS, then pushed it into phones — an indirect move that positioned Google well before the obvious battlefield (mobile apps/store).
- Why Zwishenzug: The acquisition was an unexpected intermediate positioning step that let Google shape the future mobile platform before rivals fully reacted.
- Source: Wired/NYT coverage of Android acquisition and early strategy — e.g., Wired overview: https://www.wired.com/2011/10/playbook-how-google-bought-android/

3) Amazon’s purchase of Whole Foods (2017)
- What happened: Amazon surprised many by buying a national grocery chain rather than launching a grocery chain from scratch.
- Why Zwishenzug: Acquiring an existing network and customers was a less obvious but powerful intermediate move to accelerate Amazon’s entry into brick-and-mortar groceries and logistics.
- Source: NYTimes coverage of the acquisition — https://www.nytimes.com/2017/06/16/business/dealbook/amazon-whole-foods-market.html

4) Pep Guardiola’s “false nine” usage (Barcelona, 2008–2011)
- What happened: Guardiola deployed Lionel Messi and tactical variants that abandoned a classic striker role (false nine), changing how opponents defended and creating new attacking patterns.
- Why Zwishenzug: Instead of straightforward lineup changes, the positional redefinition was an in-between tactical idea that made the later obvious actions (attacking through midfield/width) far more effective because opponents were unsettled.
- Source: Tactical analyses and reporting — e.g., The Guardian & tactical writeups: https://www.theguardian.com/football/2010/may/11/pep-guardiola-barcelona-tactics and tactical breakdowns such as https://thesefootballtimes.co/2015/10/27/how-guardiolas-barcelona-redefined-football/

5) Netflix moving to streaming while still running DVD business (mid‑2000s → 2010s)
- What happened: Netflix initially built a DVD-by-mail business but invested in streaming early and quietly pivoted, using subscription pricing and content investments before rivals fully grasped the shift.
- Why Zwishenzug: The streaming push was a preparatory, unexpected intermediate move that changed the landscape before the obvious scale-up of original content and global distribution.
- Source: Netflix corporate history and reporting: https://ir.netflix.net/ir-overview/history and industry timelines such as https://www.cnet.com/tech/services-and-software/a-brief-history-of-netflix/

Made-up / illustrative examples (plausible, for concept illustration)

6) Small-city places “pop-up” bike lanes before full redesign
- Scenario: A city installs temporary, cheap pop-up bike lanes for a season before committing to permanent street redesign.
- Why Zwishenzug: The pop-up is an intermediate, surprising action that shifts public behavior and testing, making permanent changes less resisted.

7) A job candidate emails a modest free analysis/report before the interview
- Scenario: Before an interview, a candidate sends a short (2–3 page) analysis of a company problem, not asked for, to the hiring manager.
- Why Zwishenzug: That unsolicited small deliverable changes the dynamic: the obvious next step (interview) becomes easier because the candidate already demonstrated value.

8) A retailer colors a limited-run product packaging unexpectedly before a holiday launch
- Scenario: A brand releases a small, oddly colored variant of a popular product a month before the big seasonal marketing push.
- Why Zwishenzug: The minor, surprising variant generates buzz and tests demand, so when the main seasonal campaign arrives buyers are primed and competitors are reacting to the minor earlier move.

9) A manager announces a small, nonthreatening pilot program before discussing major restructuring
- Scenario: Rather than lead with a major reorg plan, a leader first rolls out a tiny cross-team pilot with volunteers.
- Why Zwishenzug: The pilot is the intermediate move that reduces fear and provides proof, changing reactions to the later obvious restructuring.

10) A start‑up publishes an open-source toolkit before launching a paid platform
- Scenario: A company releases a small open-source library that solves a narrow pain point, then later launches a paid integrated platform.
- Why Zwishenzug: The open-source release is an unexpected positioning move that builds community, installs the product, and makes adoption of the later paid product much easier.

How to recognize or craft a Zwishenzug in life
- It’s usually small, somewhat unexpected, and makes the later obvious move easier or changes others’ expectations.
- Good Zwishenzug moves are low-cost, low-risk, and reveal new options or force your counterpart(s) to rearrange resources before the main action.

If you want, I can:
- Convert any of the made-up examples into a concrete checklist you could use in workplace or personal situations.
- Find additional vetted real-world examples in a particular domain (business, politics, sports).
